stem: What is true about dry skin (xerosis) in skin of colour?

options.html: Can appear ashen grey to red depending on the skin tone
Is always visible as white patches
Cannot occur in skin of colour

answer:
The correct answer is A.

From the vault's xerosis note (00 - Symptoms & Features). Dry skin changes colour with the background tone: it reads as ashen grey on darker skin and pink-red on lighter skin, so you look for scale, dullness and fine cracking rather than a single colour.

  • B: xerosis is not a white-patch disease; white patches suggest hypopigmentation (e.g., pityriasis alba, vitiligo).
  • C: itch is common but variable - "always severe" is wrong.
  • D: barrier dryness occurs in every skin type; the treatment (emollients to restore the barrier) is the same.

stem: What is true about erythema (redness) in skin of colour?

options.html: Always appears as a bright red rash
Can only be identified by a trained dermatologist
Can appear darker red, purple, or even black on darker skin

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Erythema is dilated, blood-filled dermal vessels seen through the epidermis; the more melanin sits on top, the more the red is masked. On darker skin inflammation therefore reads as deeper red, violaceous/purple, dusky brown or near-black, and warmth, swelling and texture become more useful than colour.

  • A: "always bright red" is the light-skin template - the reason inflammation is under-called in skin of colour.
  • B: any clinician can recognise it once they know what to look for (and palpate for warmth).
  • D: erythema can occur with or without oedema.

stem: What is true about melanoma in skin of colour?

options.html: Darker skin is completely immune to melanoma
In people with darker skin, melanoma always originates from existing moles
Melanoma in darker skin is always less aggressive than in lighter skin
People with darker skin often get melanoma in non-sun-exposed sites (mouth, soles of feet, nail unit)

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From the vault's melanoma note. In skin of colour melanoma appears in non-sun-exposed sites - the mouth, soles of the feet and the nail unit - i.e., acral lentiginous melanoma, which is not UV-driven. That is why a pigmented lesion on the sole or a new longitudinal nail band must be examined in every patient.

  • A: melanin lowers UV-driven risk but gives no immunity.
  • B: most melanomas in any skin type arise de novo, not from pre-existing moles.
  • C: the opposite - late recognition at hidden sites means diagnosis is often at a thicker, worse-prognosis stage.

stem: What is true about acne in skin of colour?

options.html: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation occurs more prominently in darker skin
Acne doesn't occur in skin of colour
Acne in skin of colour always results in scarring
People with darker skin are less prone to acne due to increased melanin production

answer:
The correct answer is A.

From the vault's post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and nodulocystic acne notes. PIH is more severe in skin of colour - lesions are darker and last longer - and PIH (with keloid scarring) is a common complication of inflammatory acne, especially in darker skin. The dark marks often bother patients more than the acne itself.

  • B: acne occurs in every skin type.
  • C: scarring is a risk, not a certainty ("always" is wrong).
  • D: melanin does not protect against acne, which is driven by sebum, follicular plugging, C. acnes and inflammation.

stem: A 35-year-old man with a history of epilepsy recently switched to the antiepileptic drug phenytoin. He presents to the emergency room with painful lesions covering her trunk, painful sores in his mouth and lips, a sore throat, fever, and fatigue. The round patches on his trunk are 2-3cm in diameter, covering about 10% of her body. The skin over the lesions sloughs off easily, and there are lesions in his mucous membranes as well. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From the vault's Stevens-Johnson syndrome and morbilliform rash notes. A new antiepileptic (phenytoin), fever and malaise, painful lesions with skin that sloughs, and mucosal involvement (mouth, lips) is a SCAR. The note defines SJS by extent: <10% BSA (TEN >30%). Management: stop the drug, burn unit/ICU, supportive care.

  • A Erythroderma: near-total body redness and scale, not 10% with sloughing and mucositis.
  • B Morbilliform eruption: phenytoin can cause it, but it is non-blistering with no mucosal disease.
  • D Contact dermatitis: itchy, confined to the contact site, no mucosa or systemic illness.

stem: A woman returns for a follow-up appointment after being treated for acne vulgaris. While her acne has cleared up, she now presents with dark spots at the previous sites of her acne lesions. This condition is known as post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH). Which of the following statements about PIH is correct?

options.html: PIH is more common in patients with lighter skin tones.
Sun exposure to inflamed areas is recommended to reduce PIH.
Early and aggressive treatment of acne can help prevent PIH.
Once PIH occurs, it is permanent and cannot fade over time.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

From the vault's post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation note. PIH follows inflammation, so the lever is less inflammation, sooner: the note says to treat inflammatory acne more aggressively (e.g., adapalene, tretinoin) and to insist on sunscreen in patients at higher risk.

  • A: backwards - PIH is more common and more severe in darker skin.
  • B: sun exposure deepens pigmentation; sunscreen is the recommendation.
  • D: without treatment it usually fades over 6-12 months (though not always), and topical retinoids or azelaic acid speed it.

stem: True or false: it’s easy to differentiate between viral vs drug induced exanthems
answer:
False, they are morphologically the same

False. A viral exanthem and a drug exanthem both typically produce a widespread, symmetric morbilliform (maculopapular) eruption; the vault's morbilliform rash note lists measles, roseola and rubella alongside phenytoin and anti-HIV drugs as causes of the same pattern. Because morphology does not discriminate, the distinction rests on the history: timing relative to a new drug, prodrome, sick contacts, and features such as an enanthem (e.g., Koplik spots) or eosinophilia.

stem: Value of skin biopsy in childhood exanthems?
answer:
Not necessary

Childhood exanthems are diagnosed clinically - the pattern of rash, its spread, the prodrome and any enanthem - and, where confirmation matters (e.g., measles for public health), by serology or PCR (the vault's measles note lists IgM serology and PCR). Histology of a viral exanthem is non-specific (a mild perivascular infiltrate), so a biopsy rarely changes management. Biopsy is reserved for the atypical or severe eruption where a SCAR (SJS/TEN) or vasculitis needs to be excluded.

lectureMeta: HippoNotes (Meds 2025 Academic Resources Team, May 2023) - the T2C question bank at the back of the document, filed under the rotation it was written for.
stem: Which is more commonly seen in pediatric clinics: specific vs non-specific viral exanthems?
answer:
Non-specific viral exanthems

"Specific" exanthems are the named, recognisable ones - measles, rubella, roseola, erythema infectiosum, varicella, hand-foot-and-mouth. Most children seen in clinic instead have a non-specific viral exanthem: a transient, blanching maculopapular rash with a mild febrile illness, caused by any of many enteroviruses or respiratory viruses, never identified, and resolving on its own. Vaccination has made several of the classic specific exanthems uncommon, which widens the gap further.

stem: State 3 clinical features of Measles infection.
answer:
Conjunctiva, Coryza, Cough

From the vault's measles note. The prodrome is the three Cs - cough, coryza (rhinorrhea) and conjunctivitis - with a high fever. Koplik spots follow on the buccal mucosa, then a rash that starts on the face and spreads downward over 2-4 days. It is airborne and highly contagious; treatment is supportive, with vitamin A for severe hospitalised cases.

stem: Name of enanthem found in Measles infection
answer:
Koplik spots

From the vault's Koplik spots and measles notes. An enanthem is a mucosal eruption (as an exanthem is a skin one). In measles it is Koplik spots: clustered, 1-3 mm whitish spots on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars, appearing 2-3 days before the rash - which makes them the clue that lets you call measles before the exanthem arrives.

stem: Important treatment for hand, foot and mouth disease
answer:
Hydration

From the vault's Coxsackie A virus note. Hand, foot and mouth disease has no specific treatment and resolves in days to weeks. The danger is the painful oral enanthem (tongue, buccal mucosa, sometimes lips and tonsils): children refuse to drink, so the note tells you to warn parents to watch for dehydration. Management is therefore hydration plus analgesia (acetaminophen/ibuprofen) so the child can drink.

stem: Management of Scarlet Fever?
answer:
Penicillin for 10 days

From the vault's Streptococcus pyogenes and penicillin V notes. Scarlet fever is Group A strep with a toxin-mediated sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue. It is treated like strep pharyngitis: penicillin V (or amoxicillin, which the S. pyogenes note lists) for a full 10 days. The full course is what matters, because the reason to treat is to prevent acute rheumatic fever (and Sydenham chorea), not only to shorten the illness. Amox-clav is reserved for beta-lactamase-positive co-infection.

stem: Out of all childhood exanthems, what is one infection that you should always remember as a medical emergency? What should you do?
answer: Meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitides. When you see fever with petechial/purpuric rash, it’s meningococcemia until proven otherwise. To work up, blood and CSF cultre should be ordered. You should provide timely treatment because it’s associated with high mortality and morbidity including hearing loss, neurologic disability, digit/limb amputation and skin scarring. You should provide 3rd generation cephalosporins along with supportive management.

stem: Atopic march (state 3).
answer:
Allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis (eczema), asthma

From the vault's atopy note. The atopic (allergic) march is the natural progression of IgE-mediated disease from infancy: atopic dermatitis (birth-1 year) → food allergy (2-3 years) → allergic rhinitis (4-6 years) → asthma (5-7 years). The three the question wants are eczema, allergic rhinitis and asthma; the key lists them out of order, but eczema comes first, which is why an eczematous infant is counselled about later asthma.

stem: Explain use of probiotics to treat atopic dermatitis

stem: Microorganism most associated with skin infection in AD? What non-medicinal remedy can be used to eradicate this infection?
answer:
Staph Aureus; bleach bath.

From the vault's atopic dermatitis note. A broken, inflamed skin barrier is readily "superinfected", most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus (weeping, crusting, sudden flare). A dilute bleach bath (sodium hypochlorite) reduces the staph load on the skin without an antibiotic, which is why it is used for recurrent infected eczema, always followed by a moisturiser to protect the barrier.

stem: Alice is a 35-year-old female coming to the ED following an event in which she fell suddenly and lost consciousness. This event was unwitnessed. Alice is unable to recall how long she was unconscious for and cannot recall anything that happened during the event. She describes walking back to her car following a yoga class when she started to feel a bit “off”. Before she knew it, she was waking up on the pavement feeling a bit groggy and disoriented. She has been living with type 1 diabetes since age 11. She takes insulin and her sugars have been well controlled for many years. She does not take any other medications. She has no significant neurological history and has never experienced an event like this before. On the physical exam, she appears pale and fatigued. All vitals are within normal range with no orthostatics changes. Heart and lung sounds are normal. No abnormal findings are noted on the neurological exam. What are your top differential diagnoses at this time? Select up to 3 answers.
answer: The correct answer is A, B, C. It’s less likely to be hyperventilation since she didn’t describe feeling anxious or breathing heavily prior; less likely to be a TIA due to the abrupt episode; less likely to be a migraine as she didn’t describe experiencing any headache or visual disturbances; less likely to be a syncope with cardiac causes because she didn’t experience any angina or palpitation prior and there are no significant cardiovascular risk factors.

stem: What should be given to Mr. Johnson to reverse the diagnosis identified above?
answer:
N-acetylcysteine

From the vault's acute liver failure note. The picture - RUQ pain, confusion, ALT/AST in the thousands, INR 6.4, rising bilirubin - is acute liver failure, and the most common cause is acetaminophen overdose. The note's specific therapy is N-acetylcysteine: it replenishes glutathione so the toxic metabolite NAPQI is detoxified. It is given even late after ingestion, and the INR is the fastest marker of improvement or worsening.

stem: Before you manage to address Mr. Johnson’s problem caused by the incompetent clerk, he describes feeling palpitations, so you order an ECG. What is the finding, and which of his medications may have triggered it?
answer: ECG finding - QT prolongation; medication - citalopram (can cause QT prolongation, particularly in the setting of acute liver failure; think antidepressants, antipsychotics, antibiotics, antifungals, antiarrhythmics, antihistamines)

stem: Ms. Lahey is an 85 year old woman presenting to the emergency room with left lower abdominal pain. She tells you that the pain began as a dull achy feeling across her entire abdomen but can now point to the pain, in her left lower quadrant. Her only surgical history is that she had her gallbladder out in 1979. With this limited history, name 3 differential diagnoses for her pain.
answer: Diverticulitis, constipation, bowel obstruction, infectious colitis, ischemic colitis, inflammatory bowel disease (bimodal age distribution, possible to be diagnosed in older ages), (ruptured) ovarian cyst, ovarian torsion, uterine fibroid, hernia, renal stones/colic, UTI; likely many others! Bad guesses - appendicitis (wrong side), ectopic pregnancy (postmenopausal)

stem: Before you can ask any more questions, Ms. Lahey suddenly feels something wet. After returning from the bathroom, she tells you that there was a lot of blood in the toilet. It was bright red and it did not hurt. You ask about cancer screening, and she tells you she did her last FIT at age 74, after which she was told she no longer required screening. She does not have a family history of colorectal cancer. You ask her about her diet, and she tells you it consists mostly of trailer park food: hot dogs, cheeseburgers, and scalloped potatoes. She is not physically active. Her current medications include atorvastatin, ramipril, aspirin, and ibuprofen. Name 2 causes of rectal bleeding, and identify the most likely cause given her presentation with left lower abdominal quadrant pain.
answer: Diverticulitis - most common cause of massive, painless, bright red rectal bleeding, and her pain, age, poor diet, and lack of physical activity support this diagnosis; others - angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids, ischemic colitis, inflammatory bowel disease, infectious colitis, colorectal cancer, post-polypectomy; likely others! Bad guesses - any cause of upper GI bleeding (would have melena)
